name: Zimmie Reva Shelton
legacy:
Graduated from Spelman College in 1929.
Spelman dedicated its admissions office to Shelton and her daughter, Jacquelyn Shelton Lee, in 2022.
biography:
Taught art in Atlanta public schools for approximately fifty years.
Saved money from her Social Security payments for her grandchildren’s education. Helped her grandson, filmmaker Shelton Jackson “Spike” Lee, attend Morehouse College and New York University.
Provided early funding for Lee’s first feature film, She’s Gotta Have It.
Married postal employee Richard Jackson Shelton, who died in 1976.

name: Jewel Woodward Simon
legacy:
Earned her undergraduate degree, summa cum laude, from Atlanta University.
Studied painting with Hale Woodruff and sculpture with Alice Dunbar.
Became the first Black graduate awarded a bachelor of fine arts degree by the Atlanta School of Art in 1967.
biography:
Taught mathematics at Jack Yates High School in Houston before settling in Atlanta with her husband, Edward Lloyd Simon.
Worked in painting, sculpture and printmaking, alongside interests in music and poetry.
Helped found the National Conference of Negro Artists and participated in Atlanta’s civic arts leadership.

name: Louie Delphia Davis Shivery
legacy: Earned a master’s degree at Atlanta University. Her 1936 thesis examined organized social work among Black Atlantans from 1890 to 1935.
biography:
Headed the English department at Booker T. Washington High School and wrote the school’s song.
Helped develop Atlanta’s Neighborhood Union and served as its executive secretary and historian.
Contributed to the Atlanta Daily World and served as president of the Atlanta Metropolitan Council of Negro Women.
Served on the board of the Colored Branch of the Atlanta Tuberculosis Association.

name: Nellie Harriet Watts
legacy: Graduated from Atlanta University and continued her education at Detroit Teachers College.
biography:
Taught in Detroit public schools and organized concert presentations featuring Black performers.
Used her own funds to bring Marian Anderson to Detroit for her first performance in the city in 1937.
Presented the Nellie Watts Concert Series for twenty-five years. Its artists included Leontyne Price, Paul Robeson and the Alvin Ailey Dance Theatre.
Founded an arts-support organization in Detroit and served on the Detroit NAACP board.
Was a daughter of South-View Cemetery co-founder Albert Watts.

name: Wilmere Kathleen Redding Adams
legacy:
Completed Atlanta University’s high school and normal teacher-training course in 1911.
Taught in Atlanta and Fulton County schools and at the Carrie Steele-Pitts Home.
biography:
Grew up on Auburn Avenue as the daughter of Wesley Chapel Redding and Ellen Redding.
Preserved local history through oral histories and her work as historian of First Congregational Church.
Served on the Auburn Avenue Research Library’s board and became known for her knowledge of Atlanta’s Black community.

name: Julia Agnes Washington Bond
legacy:
Returned to school at age fifty-six and earned a master’s degree in library science from Atlanta University.
Worked at Atlanta University’s Trevor Arnett Library and later as a part-time reference librarian at Robert W. Woodruff Library.
Retired from library work in 2000 at age ninety-two.
biography:
Attended Fisk University in Nashville, where she met educator Horace Mann Bond.
Supported her children’s civil rights work, including the organizing and public service of her son Julian Bond.

name: Minnie Dyer
legacy:
Graduated from Morris Brown College and Atlanta University before earning her teaching credentials.
Began temporary teaching work in Atlanta public schools in 1910 and joined Mitchell Street School full time in 1911.
Taught at Ashby Street School and, after retiring from public schools, at Our Lady of Lourdes Catholic School.
biography:
Worked as a seamstress before entering teaching.
Taught her niece Pearlie Craft Dove, who later became a noted educator at Clark College.
Was a daughter of Caleb and Emma Dyer. Her father, a carpenter, purchased the family’s first cemetery land at South-View.

name: Harold Irvin Bearden
legacy:
Graduated from Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
Chaired Morris Brown’s board of trustees and helped the college work toward accreditation.
biography:
Became pastor of Big Bethel AME Church in Atlanta in 1951.
Used radio sermons to speak against segregation and participated in civil rights protests.
Served as president of the Atlanta NAACP.
Was elected a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1964.

name: Fred C. Bennette Jr.
legacy:
Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
Organized against segregation at Rich’s department store while a Morris Brown student.
biography:
Served in the U.S. Army before returning to Atlanta for further education and civil rights work.
Organized voter-registration campaigns and worked closely with Martin Luther King Jr. and Andrew Young.
Became the first director of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference’s Operation Breadbasket, which challenged discriminatory employment practices.
Later advised Jimmy Carter and Andrew Young and served the King Center as an adviser and security director.

name: Hilliard D. Canady
legacy: Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary. Also studied at Meharry Medical College.
biography:
Was born in Troup County, Georgia, in 1859 and served as a presiding elder in the African Methodist Episcopal Church.
Married Nora Lee Bryant Canady, a Clark College graduate and church worker.
Their son, Hilliard D. Canady Jr., became a physician and medical inspector of Atlanta’s Black public schools. Father and son died in 1932.

name: William Alfred Fountain Sr.
legacy:
Earned degrees from Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
Served as Morris Brown’s fifth president from 1911 to 1920 and later as chancellor.
Worked alongside his son, William Alfred Fountain Jr., to sustain the college during financial hardship.
Fountain Hall, formerly Atlanta University’s Stone Hall, bears his name.
biography:
Served as an African Methodist Episcopal minister and became a bishop in 1920.
Led congregations and worked to improve their buildings and finances.
Participated in civic organizations and supported Black higher education.

name: William Alfred Fountain Jr.
legacy:
Served as Morris Brown College’s seventh president from 1929 to 1950.
Led the college through the Great Depression with support from his father, William Alfred Fountain Sr., who served as chancellor.
Chose to take no salary during the financial crisis while Morris Brown reorganized to remain open.
During his administration, Morris Brown joined the Atlanta University Center and relocated to the former Atlanta University campus.
biography: After leaving Morris Brown, served as secretary-treasurer of the African Methodist Episcopal Church’s General Board of Education.

name: Evelyn Jones Frazier
legacy: Earned a bachelor’s degree from Morris Brown College in 1952 while developing her restaurant business.
biography:
Opened the Evelyn Jones Cafe in 1936. Expanded the business with her husband, Luther Ellis Frazier, in the 1940s as Frazier’s Cafe Society.
Provided a meeting place for Black civic, religious and civil rights organizations. Patrons included Benjamin Mays, Martin Luther King Jr. and Thurgood Marshall.
Supported businesswomen’s organizations and the NAACP.

name: Cornelius King
legacy: Served as a trustee of Morris Brown College.
biography:
Worked in Atlanta’s private clubs and later in Washington, D.C., before establishing businesses serving Black Atlantans.
Opened King’s Wigwam, a recreation resort near Kennesaw, in 1918.
Helped organize Mercy Hospital in 1919 and served as its superintendent.
Founded Cornelius King & Son real estate in 1922. His son Turner later headed the family firm.
Chaired Big Bethel AME Church’s trustees. His second wife, Nina Culver King, was a Spelman graduate.

name: John Henry Lewis
legacy:
Graduated from Morris Brown College in 1905 and later joined its faculty.
Served as the college’s sixth president from 1920 to 1928.
Returned as its eighth president in 1951 and remained in office until his death in 1958.
biography:
Studied ministry at Yale Divinity School and pursued graduate education at the University of Chicago.
Served as an African Methodist Episcopal minister and educational administrator in several states.
Led Dunbar High School and Shorter College and served as dean of Payne Theological Seminary.
Was the father of historian David Levering Lewis.

name: John Wesley Edward Linder
legacy: Graduated from Morris Brown College and continued his medical education at Meharry Medical College.
biography:
Began practicing medicine in Dublin, Georgia, before relocating to Atlanta.
Served as president of the Atlanta Medical Association and Georgia Medical Association, professional organizations for Black physicians.
Established the Georgia Medical Association’s first quarterly journal.
Served on the National Medical Association’s executive board.

name: Henry James Charles Bowden
legacy:
Graduated from Morehouse College in 1925.
Continued his education at General Theological Seminary and Columbia University.
biography:
Was ordained an Episcopal priest in 1929 and became rector of St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Atlanta in 1934.
Served as a military and Veterans Administration chaplain.
Worked with aging-service organizations and the NAACP, advocating for older adults.
Fulton County’s H. J. C. Bowden senior multipurpose facility was named in recognition of his work.

name: Clifford Nathaniel Ellis
legacy:
Completed Morehouse Academy before graduating from Morehouse College in 1926.
Earned a divinity degree from the Morehouse School of Religion in 1927.
biography:
Pastored churches in Georgia and led Reed Street, later Paradise, Baptist Church for more than four decades.
Extended the church’s reach through the Chariot Wheels gospel radio broadcast.
Served as president of the Atlanta Baptist Ministers Union and on the National Baptist Convention’s board.
Married Vashti Scott Ellis, a journalist in the Atlanta Daily World publishing family.

name: Charles Walter Greenlea
legacy: Graduated from Morehouse College and earned a master’s degree from Atlanta University.
biography:
Served for twenty years as executive director of the Atlanta NAACP.
Worked as an editor at the Atlanta Daily World and with Economic Opportunity Atlanta.
Co-founded and led Summerhill Neighborhood Inc., working on housing and neighborhood development.
Greenlea Commons in Summerhill was named in his honor.

name: Rogers Henderson
legacy:
Was named an honorary alumnus of Morehouse College in recognition of his support.
With his wife, contributed a stained-glass window and painting to Morehouse’s Danforth Chapel.
biography:
Founded Henderson Realty Company on Auburn Avenue and helped establish the Empire Real Estate Board.
Worked with his wife, Ida Franklin Henderson, who joined the business and held leadership roles in Black women’s civic organizations.

name: Charles Dubois Hubert
legacy:
Completed Morehouse Academy in 1905 and earned a bachelor’s degree from Morehouse College in 1909.
Taught church history and directed the college’s School of Religion.
Served as acting president from 1937 to 1940, between the administrations of Samuel Archer and Benjamin Mays.
biography:
Earned a divinity degree from Rochester Theological Seminary in 1912.
Served as pastor of Providence Baptist Church while working in higher education.

name: Dennis Taylor Hubert
legacy:
Was a divinity student at Morehouse College when he was killed in 1930.
Morehouse honored his life at its 2025 commencement with a posthumous honorary bachelor’s degree.
biography:
Was eighteen when a white mob killed him on the Crogman School playground in Atlanta on June 15, 1930.
Was the son of minister Gaddus Johnson Hubert and educator Pearl Parks Hubert, and a nephew of Morehouse leader Charles Dubois Hubert.
His family faced further attacks after his killing.

name: Graham Washington Jackson
legacy: Attended Morehouse College and Atlanta University.
biography:
Performed on piano, organ and accordion and led music at Booker T. Washington High School.
Played at wartime fundraising events and performed for U.S. presidents.
Became widely known through a 1945 photograph showing him playing the accordion in mourning for Franklin Roosevelt.
Led jazz ensembles, worked in broadcasting and performed at Atlanta venues.
Was named Georgia’s official state musician by Governor Jimmy Carter.

name: Phoebe Lucille Fraser Burney Callier Hart
legacy:
Graduated from Clark College in 1935 and pursued religious-education study at Gammon Theological Seminary.
Worked in Morehouse College’s endowment office before becoming Clark’s dean of women.
Served as dean of women at Clark College from 1943 to 1958.
biography:
Directed religious education for the southeastern region of the Congregational church.
Later known as Phoebe Callier, served educational institutions in Chattanooga.
Sponsored two children from Africa and helped bring them to the United States.

name: Cora B. Finley
legacy:
Graduated from Spelman and became its first alumna to earn an advanced degree at Atlanta University.
Served as principal of Atlanta’s Yonge Street School and later led the education department at Alabama State University.
biography:
Helped organize an early Black parent-teacher association in 1911.
Challenged unequal teacher salaries through the Gate City Teachers Association.
Worked with the NAACP and served on the Atlanta Urban League’s first board.
Organized a night school for Black Atlantans.

name: Estelle B. Ivey
legacy: Graduated from Spelman’s historical nursing school.
biography:
Grew up with her four brothers in the Carrie Steele orphanage after their parents died.
Worked as bookkeeper, secretary and treasurer of Ivey Brothers Funeral Home, established by her brothers Henry and James in 1912.
Helped operate a family business known for supporting churches, charitable work and families with limited financial means.

name: Clara Ivey Wilson
legacy:
Graduated from Spelman College in 1938.
Spelman’s Ivey-Wilson endowed scholarship was established in her memory.
biography:
Succeeded her father, Henry M. Ivey, in ownership and leadership of Ivey Brothers Funeral Home.
Served on South-View Cemetery’s board and became its second vice president.
Worked with Gate City Day Nurseries and Delta Sigma Theta and served on a Fulton County jury in 1962.

name: Nina Culver King
legacy: Graduated from Spelman College.
biography:
Worked in the United States Patent Office in Washington, D.C., where she met Cornelius King.
Became King’s second wife. He served as a Morris Brown trustee and established businesses serving Black Atlantans.

name: Alberta Williams King
legacy:
Graduated from Spelman Seminary’s high school program in 1922.
Continued her education at Hampton and earned a bachelor’s degree from Morris Brown College in 1938.
Spelman’s Alberta Williams King Memorial Endowed Scholarship supports music and nonviolence studies.
biography:
Led Ebenezer Baptist Church’s choir and served for decades as organist and music director.
Raised her family with Martin Luther King Sr. and was the mother of Martin Luther King Jr.
Was the daughter of Ebenezer pastor Adam Daniel Williams and Jennie Celeste Williams.
Was killed while playing the church organ during Sunday worship in June 1974.

name: Flora Ethelwyn Zeto Malekebu
legacy:
Graduated from Spelman’s high school program in 1915, becoming its first African graduate.
Spelman’s Gordon-Zeto Center for Global Education was named in part for her.
biography:
Came from the Congo to Atlanta as a child with Spelman alumna and missionary Clara A. Howard.
Married physician Daniel Sharpe Malekebu, who had come from Africa with a missionary and later trained at Meharry Medical College.
Worked with her husband in African missions and maintained connections with supporters in the United States.
Served as an assistant at Providence Industrial Mission in Nyasaland.
